about.story:
RADIANCE Dermatology & Aesthetics Clinic has a simple mission: to help every individual feel confident in their skin. We combine medical dermatology, hair and scalp care and aesthetic treatments in one welcoming place in Freetown.

We believe healthy skin starts with understanding it, so education sits alongside treatment: in the clinic, in our awareness campaigns, and in the RADIANCE patient app.
about.quote: Radiant skin is a journey, not a destination

services.name: Medical dermatology
services.short: Assessment of skin, hair and nail concerns by the clinical team.
services.overview: A first consultation for any skin, hair or nail concern you'd like checked. The clinician takes a history, examines the area and explains what they think is going on and what the options are.
concerns: Changes in a mole or mark
services.involves: A conversation about when the problem started and what you've tried, an examination, and a plan you agree on together. Some conditions need a test or a follow-up visit before a diagnosis is clear.
services.inPerson: Most skin conditions are best assessed in person, where the clinician can see the skin in good light and examine it.
faq: Ask the clinic when you book. Bring any letters or results you already have.
Your current skincare and medicines (or photos of the labels), and a short timeline of the problem.

services.name: Acne & acne scarring
services.short: Care for breakouts and the marks or scars they leave.
services.overview: Acne is common at every age and in every skin tone. Treatment depends on the type of spots, how widespread they are and how your skin reacts, and it usually takes weeks to months to judge.
services.involves: Examination of the affected areas, a review of products you use, and a stepwise plan. Prescription treatments are only started after a clinician assesses you.
services.inPerson: Deep, painful or scarring acne should be seen in person early, because early treatment reduces the risk of permanent scars.
faq: Most acne treatments take 8–12 weeks to show their effect. Your clinician will tell you what to expect for your plan.

services.name: Hyperpigmentation & uneven tone
services.short: Dark marks, patches and uneven-looking skin tone.
services.overview: Darker patches can follow spots, irritation, sun exposure or hormonal changes. Some fade on their own; others need treatment. Working out the cause matters, because the right approach differs.
concerns: Patches on the cheeks or forehead
services.involves: An examination, a look at your routine and sun habits, and a plan that avoids irritation. Products of unknown origin that promise fast lightening can contain mercury or strong steroids; bring them so the clinician can check.
services.inPerson: A patch that is changing, raised, bleeding or itchy should be examined in person.

services.name: Eczema & psoriasis
services.short: Dry, itchy, inflamed skin and reactions to products.
services.overview: Eczema and dermatitis cover several conditions that make skin dry, itchy and inflamed. Triggers can include soaps, fragrances, heat, sweat and specific ingredients.
services.involves: A history of flares and triggers, an examination, and a plan for both settling the current flare and preventing the next one.
services.inPerson: Skin that is weeping, crusting, very painful or spreading quickly should be seen promptly.

services.name: Rashes & allergies
services.short: Red, itchy or burning rashes, including skin-fold rashes (intertrigo) and reactions.
services.overview: Rashes in skin folds, such as under the breasts, in the groin, armpits or between the thighs, are common in warm, humid weather. Friction and moisture irritate the skin, and yeast or bacteria can join in.
concerns: Darkened or thickened skin in folds
services.involves: An examination to tell irritation from infection or another condition, because they look alike and need different care.
services.inPerson: If the rash has an odour, oozes, spreads or keeps returning, get it checked rather than trying more products.

services.name: Skin cancer screening
services.short: Early detection saves lives: checks of moles and changing marks.
services.overview: A skin check looks at moles, spots and marks that are new, changing, bleeding or different from the rest. Skin cancer can occur in every skin tone, including on the palms, soles and under the nails, which are commonly affected in darker skin.
services.involves: A full or targeted skin examination, and a plan if anything needs watching, testing or removing.
services.inPerson: Any mole or mark that is changing, bleeding, itchy or new should be examined in person. Photos can't rule out skin cancer.

services.name: Hair loss treatment
services.short: Finding out why hair is thinning, shedding or falling out in patches.
services.overview: Hair loss isn't one thing. Alopecia areata, traction alopecia, pattern hair loss and shedding after illness or stress all look different and need different plans. The sooner it's checked, the better the outcome.
concerns: Thinning at the hairline or temples
Hair loss with a sore or itchy scalp
services.involves: A history of when it started and your styling, an examination of the scalp and hair, and sometimes tests. You'll leave knowing what's likely going on and what the options are.
services.inPerson: Sudden or patchy hair loss, or hair loss with pain, redness or scarring, should be assessed in person soon.
faq: Can a photo tell what kind of hair loss I have?
No. Photos help track change over time, but the cause needs a clinician's examination and history.

services.name: Traction alopecia
services.short: Hair loss from tension: braids, weaves, wigs and tight styles.
services.overview: Repeated pulling on the same hair, especially at the hairline and temples, can thin it over time. Caught early, it often improves once the tension stops.
concerns: Styles that feel tight for days
services.involves: An examination of the hairline and scalp and practical advice on styling that protects your hair.
services.inPerson: Long-standing thinning can become permanent, so earlier assessment helps.

services.name: Scalp conditions
services.short: Flaking, itching, tenderness and scalp rashes.
services.overview: Dandruff, dryness, product buildup and several skin conditions can all cause flakes and itch. They look alike, and they need different care.
services.involves: An examination of the scalp and a look at your wash routine and products.
services.inPerson: Painful, weeping or crusted areas, or scalp problems with hair loss, should be examined.

services.name: Hair breakage & damage
services.short: Breakage, dryness and damage from chemicals or heat.
services.overview: Breakage along the length is different from hair falling out from the root. Relaxers, colour, heat and handling all play a part, and so can some medical conditions.
services.involves: A look at the hair shaft and scalp, your styling history and routine, and a plan to reduce further damage.
services.inPerson: If you're not sure whether hair is breaking or shedding, an examination can tell.

services.name: Aesthetic consultation
services.short: A medical conversation about elective skin treatments.
services.overview: An aesthetic consultation is a chance to talk about how you'd like your skin to look and whether a treatment is suitable for you. Suitability depends on your skin, health and expectations, and a qualified professional must assess you first.
concerns: Questions about treatments you've heard of
services.involves: An assessment of your skin, a frank discussion of benefits, risks, recovery and alternatives, and time to decide. No treatment is pressured on the day.
services.inPerson: All aesthetic treatments require an in-person assessment.
faq: Ask the clinic. This website lists specific procedures only once the clinic confirms them.

services.name: PRP therapy
services.short: A treatment option for some types of hair loss, after assessment.
services.overview: Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) uses a concentrate from your own blood, injected into the scalp. It may help some kinds of hair loss and not others, so it's only considered after the cause has been assessed.
services.involves: A hair loss assessment first. If PRP is suitable, the clinician explains the number of sessions, what to expect, side effects and alternatives.
services.inPerson: Requires an in-person assessment and treatment in the clinic.

services.name: Hair restoration
services.short: Long-term plans to support regrowth and protect existing hair.
services.overview: Hair restoration covers the treatments and changes that help regrowth and protect the hair you have. The right plan depends entirely on the type of hair loss.
services.involves: Assessment of the cause, then a plan that may combine treatments, styling changes and follow-up photos.

services.name: Botox & fillers
services.short: Injectable treatments to smooth, refresh and enhance.
services.overview: Anti-wrinkle injections and dermal fillers are medical treatments. Whether they suit you depends on your health, skin and goals, and on an honest discussion of risks and results.
services.involves: A consultation covering suitability, risks, recovery, aftercare and alternatives before any treatment. You can take time to decide.
services.inPerson: Must be assessed and performed in person by a qualified professional.

services.name: Chemical peels
services.short: Renewing the skin's surface for tone and texture.
services.overview: A chemical peel applies a solution that removes the outer layers of skin. In deeper skin tones, peel choice and strength matter, because the wrong peel can cause dark marks.
services.involves: Assessment of your skin and history, a patch or test area if needed, and clear aftercare including sun protection.

services.name: Microneedling
services.short: Supporting collagen for texture and scarring.
services.overview: Microneedling makes tiny controlled punctures in the skin to stimulate repair. It's used for some acne scars and texture concerns.
services.involves: An assessment of suitability, the number of sessions usually needed, downtime and aftercare.
services.inPerson: Must be assessed and performed in person.

services.name: Laser treatments
services.short: Targeted treatments, chosen for your skin type.
services.overview: Lasers can treat some pigmentation, hair and texture concerns. Laser type and settings must suit your skin tone to avoid burns or dark marks.
services.involves: An assessment of whether a laser is the right tool for you, a test patch if needed, and aftercare.
services.inPerson: Must be assessed and performed in person.

articles.title: Hair loss isn't one thing
articles.summary: Alopecia areata, traction alopecia and pattern hair loss look different and need different plans.
body: "Alopecia" simply means hair loss. There are many kinds, and the right plan depends on which one you have.
Alopecia areata usually causes round, smooth patches of hair loss that can appear quickly. It happens when the immune system targets hair follicles. Hair often regrows, and treatments can help.

Traction alopecia comes from repeated pulling on the hair, often at the hairline and temples, from tight braids, weaves, wigs, ponytails or extensions. Caught early, it often improves once the tension stops; left for years it can become permanent.
Pattern hair loss causes gradual thinning, typically at the crown or parting in women and at the temples and crown in men. It tends to run in families and responds best to early treatment.
Shedding can also increase a few months after illness, childbirth, surgery or major stress, and with some medicines and nutritional problems.
Because these look alike to the untrained eye, and because some types scar, getting an examination early gives you the best chance of keeping your hair.

articles.title: Rashes in skin folds: intertrigo
articles.summary: Why warm, moist skin folds get irritated, and when to get it checked.
body: Intertrigo is inflammation where two areas of skin rub together: under the breasts, in the groin, armpits, between the thighs or in neck folds.
Heat, sweat and friction break down the skin's surface. The area becomes red, itchy, sore or burning, and in deeper skin tones may look darker or purplish rather than red.
Yeast or bacteria often take advantage of the damaged skin, which is why some rashes smell, ooze or keep coming back.

Keeping folds dry, wearing breathable fabrics and avoiding harsh soaps can help. But other conditions look similar, so a rash that doesn't settle, spreads, or keeps returning is worth having examined rather than trying product after product.

articles.title: Skin type, sensitivity and dehydration are different things
articles.summary: Why your skin profile asks about each one separately.
body: Skin type describes how much oil your skin tends to produce: oily, dry, combination or balanced. It's fairly stable, though it can shift with age, climate and hormones.
Sensitivity is about how easily skin reacts with stinging, burning, itching or redness. Oily skin can be sensitive; dry skin can be robust.
Dehydration describes skin that feels tight or looks dull because it's low in water. Any skin type can feel dehydrated, including oily skin.
Allergy is different again: an immune reaction to a specific ingredient, such as fragrance or a preservative. A dermatologist can confirm it with patch testing.
Keeping these separate helps you choose products more precisely and helps your clinician understand your history.

articles.title: Sunscreen for every skin tone
articles.summary: Deeper skin still benefits from daily protection, especially for dark marks.
body: UV exposure contributes to sun damage and skin cancer in every skin tone, though the risk and how damage shows up differ.
For people prone to dark marks after breakouts or irritation, UV and visible light can make those marks darker or last longer. Daily sunscreen is one of the most consistently recommended steps.
Broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher is a common recommendation. Mineral filters can leave a white cast on deeper skin; tinted formulas are often easier to wear.
Most people apply too little. About two finger-lengths for the face and neck is a common rule of thumb. Reapply after swimming, sweating or long periods outdoors.

articles.title: Dark marks after spots: what helps
articles.summary: Marks left after breakouts often fade slowly over months.
body: Darker marks left after a spot or irritation are very common, particularly in medium and deep skin tones. They usually fade on their own over months.
The most useful steps are generally preventing new breakouts and irritation, avoiding picking, and daily sun protection.

Ingredients such as azelaic acid, niacinamide, vitamin C and retinoids appear in products aimed at uneven-looking tone. Harsh scrubs and strong combinations can backfire by causing irritation that leads to more marks.

If marks are widespread or you aren't sure what they are, a dermatologist can tell you and offer treatments not available over the counter. Avoid products of unknown origin that promise fast lightening; some contain mercury or high-strength steroids.

articles.title: Hair porosity, without the myths
articles.summary: What porosity is, and why a photo or a glass of water can't measure it.
body: Porosity describes how easily water and products move into and out of the hair shaft. It's influenced by the condition of the cuticle, the outer layer of the hair.
Chemical treatments, bleach and heat tend to raise porosity, and ends are often more porous than roots because they're older.
The popular float test isn't reliable on its own: oils, product residue and surface tension change whether a strand floats.

A better guide is how your hair behaves over time: how quickly it wets and dries, whether products absorb or sit on top, and how long moisture lasts. Treat any result as a tendency, not a fixed label.

articles.title: Density vs strand thickness
articles.summary: How much hair you have is different from how thick each strand is.
body: Density is how many strands grow on your scalp: low, medium or high. You can see it by how much scalp shows when hair is parted or pulled back.
Strand thickness is the width of a single hair: fine, medium or coarse. You can compare one strand to a sewing thread between your fingers.
It's common to have high density with fine strands, or low density with coarse strands. Both affect which products feel heavy and how styles hold.
Coily and tightly textured hair can show more scalp at certain angles and shrinks considerably, so photos of density should always be taken the same way each time.

articles.title: Protective styles without the pull
articles.summary: Tension is the main thing to watch around the hairline.
body: Braids, locs, weaves, wigs and tight ponytails can protect ends and reduce daily handling, but repeated tension on the same follicles, especially at the hairline and temples, can lead to thinning over time.
Warning signs include pain, tenderness, small bumps at the base of braids, or a style that still feels tight after a few days.
Lighter, looser installs, varying where tension falls, and breaks between styles all reduce strain. Edges usually benefit from the least tension and heat.
Early hairline thinning from tension is often reversible if caught early. If you notice it, book an assessment.

articles.title: Flakes, itch and buildup
articles.summary: Several different things look similar on the scalp.
body: Flaking can come from dry skin, product buildup, infrequent washing, or common skin conditions that need specific treatment. They can look alike in photos.
Buildup often improves with a thorough or clarifying wash. Dryness often improves with gentler cleansing.
Persistent flaking with redness, greasy yellowish scale, itching that disturbs sleep, sores, or patches of hair loss are reasons to see a dermatologist rather than keep trying products.

articles.title: Introducing new products safely
articles.summary: One at a time, and patch test first.
body: Introducing one new product at a time, with a week or two in between, makes it much easier to tell what suits you and what doesn't.

A simple home patch test: apply a little of the product to a small area, such as behind the ear or the inner arm, once or twice a day for several days and watch for redness, itching or swelling. It doesn't rule out every reaction.
Strong actives such as retinoids and exfoliating acids are usually started a few times a week, building up slowly.
If you react, stop the product, write down what happened, and contact the clinic or a pharmacist if it doesn't settle.

articles.title: When to see a dermatologist
articles.summary: Signs that a skin, hair or nail problem needs a professional look.
body: Book an appointment if a skin problem hasn't improved after a few weeks of sensible care, keeps coming back, or is affecting your sleep, work or confidence.
Get seen soon for a mole or mark that is new, changing, bleeding or different from your others; sudden or patchy hair loss; or a rash that is spreading, painful or blistering.
Seek urgent care for a rapidly spreading painful red area with fever, widespread blistering or peeling skin, or swelling of the face, lips or tongue, especially with difficulty breathing.
Photos and apps can help you keep a record, but they can't replace an examination.

articles.title: Getting the most from your appointment
articles.summary: Bring a timeline, products and your questions.
body: Appointments are short. A clear history helps: when the problem started, how it has changed, what you've tried, and what made it better or worse.
Bring a list of products with ingredients, or the packaging. Photos taken in similar light over time are useful, particularly for things that come and go.
Write your questions down beforehand and put the most important first.
Ask how long before you should expect a change, what side effects to watch for, and when to come back.
